title: Mandelson, Epstein, and the Lure of the Rich
author: Donald Macintyre
content:
_**A note from our Editor-in-Chief:**_

_The huge story in the UK over the last week was the arrest of former Labour
Party grandee and former British ambassador to Trump 's Washington, Peter
Mandelson. But what does it all mean for the Labour Party and Prime Minister
Keir Starmer? And why did Mandelson end up so close to Jeffrey Epstein? Who
better to lay it out for us than Donald Macintyre, the acclaimed British
journalist who wrote a biography of Mandelson back in 1999? **Zeteo** is
privileged to have Macintyre writing for us, so do please become a **[paid
subscriber](http://zeteo.com/subscribe)** to support our independent
journalism. _

_**-Mehdi**_

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd43d6e85-2aed-42f7-827a-c551ec98c173_1874x1136.jpeg)
_Peter Mandelson leaves his home in Wiltshire on Feb. 20, 2026. Photo by Ben
Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images_

If nothing else, the arrest last Monday of Peter Mandelson, long one of the
most powerful figures in British politics, is a reminder that the UK
authorities have acted more decisively than those in the US against at least
two public figures who were entangled with the global financier, pedophile,
and procurer Jeffrey Epstein. It's true that police investigations of both the
former Prince Andrew and Mandelson, Britain's former ambassador to the US, do
not concern Epstein's disgusting exploitation of young girls. Rather, they are
into the allegations of the two men's transmission and exploitation of inside
information when they were caught in Epstein's web while also acting as public
servants, in Mandelson's case as a key member of Gordon Brown's Cabinet
between 2008 and 2010, including as Brown's de facto deputy.

That said, Mandelson's fall has proved a seismic event for the Labour
government.

It would be too crude to blame it for[ Labour's catastrophic by-election
defeat by the Greens](https://zeteo.com/p/uk-green-party-won-historic-victory)
in the Greater Manchester constituency of Gorton and Denton, though it
certainly didn't help. But it is relevant to that defeat in at least two ways.
The first is that Mandelson represented - and in many respects had come to
symbolize the most right-wing, and arguably most cynical, stream in Labour
politics, against which the Gorton and Denton voters so spectacularly revolted
- from the left - on Thursday. The second is that Keir Starmer's leadership -
about which the defeat is bound to fuel fresh speculation - might have been
less vulnerable if he had not already faced calls to step down over his
decision to appoint Mandelson as ambassador to Washington back in December
2024. Starmer has repeatedly
[said](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/feb/04/starmer-confirms-he-
knew-mandelson-kept-epstein-ties-after-prison-term) that Mandelson lied about
the depth of his friendship with Epstein when he was a candidate for the job.

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb22b2b5e-3870-4c1d-9fc3-fe1369589384_1500x921.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8anv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb22b2b5e-3870-4c1d-9fc3-fe1369589384_1500x921.jpeg)_Peter
Mandelson and Jeffrey Epstein in an undated photo released by the US
Department of Justice._

We won't know exactly what Mandelson said back then, unless the [government
fulfils its promise](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/uk-government-agrees-
with-police-release-documents-related-
mandelsons-2026-02-26/#:~:text=Reuters%20Plus-,UK%20government%20agrees%20framework%20on%20publishing%20Mandelson%20vetting%20documents,Sign%20up%20here.)
to release the documentation around the appointment. But either way, he was
appointed when it was public knowledge that he remained an Epstein associate
after the latter's first criminal conviction in 2008.

### **The Final Fracture in New Labour**

Throughout his political career, Mandelson has shown an uncanny ability to
come back from what seemed like the political dead. That includes in 1998,
after he resigned from one Cabinet post having been found to have secretly
accepted a [$625,000 low-interest home
loan](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1998-dec-24-mn-57266-story.html)
from his millionaire fellow MP Geoffrey Robinson, and again in 2001, when it
was revealed he intervened briefly in the passport application by wealthy,
prominent Indian businessman Srichand Hinduja. As Mandelson put it when he was
returned as MP for Hartlepool after the two resignations: "I'm a fighter, not
a quitter." But now his comeback abilities have finally run out of road.****
And that, in turn, marks the final fracture of New Labour, the banner under
which Labour fought the 1997 election with such success and, indeed, continued
to govern. Mandelson was, with Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, the third man of
the "modernizing" trio behind its success, built in large part on extending
Labour's appeal to voters in the center ground. For all the continued rows and
ruptures over that period, usually between Brown, instinctively the least
centrist and most social democratic of the group, and the others, it had been
one of the most potent forces in British politics since World War II.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v9Mu!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd8fefe30-a0af-4fce-a85c-e86f318f4eb5_3000x1941.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!v9Mu!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd8fefe30-a0af-4fce-a85c-e86f318f4eb5_3000x1941.jpeg)_Gordon
Brown and Peter Mandelson in May 2010. Photo by Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images_

Now look where we are. Brown, of the trio the least interested in making
money, feels betrayed by Mandelson's market-sensitive leaks to Epstein in real
time when he was struggling to stabilize the British economy in the wake of
the financial crash (not to mention by Mandelson's invitation to JP Morgan to
"threaten" the government over its plans to curb bankers' bonuses). He has led
the charge against Mandelson and Andrew, and the degradation of politics he
sees their actions as representing, even supplying much of the information the
police are now sifting through. And Blair has remained conspicuously silent.
You can't help wondering if Blair is conscious that Mandelson, in seeking the
big bucks after leaving office, as his emails with Epstein suggest he was, was
rather following in his own footsteps. Indeed, Mandelson's emails imply that
he was after a role with JP Morgan, which just happens to be where Blair slung
his hook at a reported [$1 million a
year](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2008/jan/10/blairjpmorgan) shortly
after stepping down as premier.

For Mandelson, the lure of the rich seems not to have played much part until
his 40s, when he started to meet important business figures who correctly
identified him, after 1994, as close to Blair, recently anointed as the new
Labour leader. That was accentuated by his period as Trade and Industry
secretary under Blair, when he started to meet a wider range of millionaire
business leaders, including in the US, enjoying, for example, transatlantic
flights, and at least one stay in Long Island with the lingerie boss Linda
Wachner.

Either way, the US Justice Department-released exchanges are illustrative. On
the one hand Mandelson shares with Epstein his anxiety about how "I am going
to earn my living" when Labour leaves office (at a time when he was earning
£104,000 as a Cabinet minister, potentially in line for an, over time, seven
digit severance and pension payment from his job as an EU commissioner and
could presumably have had, as an immediately ex-Cabinet minister, the pick of
decent UK jobs, if not as good as those he was apparently seeking in what
Epstein calls in one of his own emails "moneyland"). On the other hand, in one
of his own frequent exchanges with Epstein, a seemingly envious former Israeli
Prime Minister, Ehud Barak, reports his wonder at what Epstein calls the
"gigantic" multi-million consultancy fees being earned by Blair across the
globe.

### **The McSweeney Factor**

There's another reverberation from the Mandelson scandal. The departure of his
protege, Morgan McSweeney, as Starmer's chief of staff (because he had most
forcefully recommended the appointment of Mandelson to Washington) has removed
what many Labour MPs see as the leading conduit of Mandelsonian influence.
This goes back to Starmer's chameleon-like embrace in his 2020 contest for the
party leadership of a sub-Corbynite, left-wing agenda that he and those around
him had zero intention of carrying out. Blair, who, arguably to his credit,
donned no such disguise when he stood in 1994 for the leadership, was
privately appalled by this cynical approach. Mandelson was - to use a
Mandelsonian word - "relaxed" about it.

Once he became leader, of course, Starmer, showing an abnormally high
dependency, to put it mildly, on his leading adviser, swung the pendulum back
as far as it would go. The brilliance with which Starmer [repeatedly
credited](https://www.itn.co.uk/news/pm-morgan-mcsweeney-helped-me-win-
election) McSweeney for a landslide election victory - achieved largely by
ruthless targeting of resources to offset a historically low vote share, for a
victorious party, [of just under
34%](https://researchbriefings.files.parliament.uk/documents/CBP-10009/CBP-10009.pdf)
- was not matched by anything remotely like the preparations for actual
governing that had been undertaken by Blair and Brown. But that was not all.
The party went into the election with a promise - by which it has since been
hamstrung - not to raise income tax. This may have made sense in the
relatively buoyant economic circumstances confronted by New Labour when Blair
was elected in 1997. Whether forsaking the most progressive means of raising
revenue - especially among the higher paid - to deal with the dire state of
public services, did so in the 2020s is much more doubtful.

Moreover, the half-baked cuts in pensioner and disabled benefits - in the
notable absence of a comprehensive welfare reform program and subsequently
rejected by Labour MPs - seemed like an almost gratuitous attempt to reinforce
the idea that this was no left-wing, or even left of center, government. As
did the drive against immigration and asylum, for which many in the party also
blamed McSweeney, which has seemingly approached the threat to Labour posed by
the hard-right Reform UK by being more like Reform.

And so, on some aspects of foreign policy. After his draconian purge of
antisemitic elements in the party, Starmer might have decided that it gave him
space to adopt a more critical position towards Israel's conduct of the Gaza
war. There were good electoral as well as moral reasons for doing so,
underscored by the[ switch of Muslim and other
voters](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/feb/27/gorton-and-
denton-byelection-keir-starmer-labour) from Labour to the Greens on Thursday.
Instead, having refused even to join international calls for a ceasefire in
opposition, he was finally dragged last year by party unrest into recognition
of a Palestinian state. It's hard, of course, to detect on this issue, as well
as others, where Mandelson's influence ends and McSweeney's begins. But there
is an instructive exchange of emails between Mandelson, while he was still
ambassador, and Health Secretary Wes Streeting. Streeting, very much not on
the party's left, argues in [July
2025](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/feb/09/streeting-wrote-off-
his-re-election-chances-in-whatsapp-exchanges-with-mandelson) for recognition,
[telling](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/feb/09/streeting-wrote-
off-his-re-election-chances-in-whatsapp-exchanges-with-mandelson) Mandelson
that Israel "is committing war crimes before our eyes." Mandelson differs,
offering the standard argument that recognition might blow a two-state
solution "out of the water" by triggering annexation of the West Bank, which
the US would be "powerless to stop." With good reason, Streeting responds:
"Israel is doing it anyway. This is rogue state behaviour."

corruption?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjozNjIwMjc3ODksInBvc3RfaWQiOjE4OTM5MDk5NywiaWF0IjoxNzcyNjQ1NDU1LCJleHAiOjE3NzUyMzc0NTUsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0yMzI1NTExIiwic3ViIjoicG9zdC1yZWFjdGlvbiJ9.-orZ0HwmF8vU7GKUEhdeowyYBqR7p-tHT9CZEdIyxRQ)

The question, therefore, is whether the vacuum left most directly by
McSweeney's exit will leave room for efforts to make the Starmer
administration look a little more like a Labour government. As it happens,
there is something popular that Starmer could do - to put in train the anti-
corruption agenda [laid out by Gordon
Brown](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/feb/06/peter-mandelson-
jeffrey-epstein-victims-democracy-change-gordon-
brown#:~:text=First%2C%20we%20need%20an%20independent%20anti%2Dcorruption%20commission,to%20remove%20all%20doubt%20as%20to%20our)
in the wake of the Mandelson saga. One of these is a major curb on lobbying -
an important corrective for a party that has often made a virtue out of its
dependence on large donations, personal and corporate, and the access they
afford. And another, even simpler, is the extension of US-style pre-
appointment hearings for top government appointments - including, but not
limited to, senior ambassadors - by cross-party parliamentary committees. In
some ways, these could be even more effective than those of their US
congressional counterparts, by being less beholden to the executive than the
latter-at least at present, tend to be. It is the safest bet that, had
Mandelson had to appear before such a committee in December 2024, his
appointment would not have been approved. (And if parliamentarians could have
overcome the inhibitions against policing the royals - as they will surely now
have to do in future - it's highly unlikely that former Prince Andrew would
have been made an official trade envoy back in 2001.)

By publicly insisting on Tuesday that the Metropolitan Police only [arrested
Mandelson](https://zeteo.com/p/getting-away-with-epstein-first-draft) - in
preference to a voluntary interview to which they say he would have readily
assented - because of a false belief that he might flee the country, his
lawyers have given more than a hint that he will fight the accusations that he
committed misconduct in public life. But even if he were to escape
prosecution, let alone conviction, that will hardly undermine the need, so
forcibly underlined by Thursday's by-election result, for a major Starmer
reset. A serious drive to clean up politics would be a start.

_**Donald Macintyre** is an award-winning journalist and writer who was
formerly political editor and chief political commentator for The Independent
in the UK. He is the author of 'Mandelson: The Biography.'_
